title: Hohosboco / Spring Creek area
summary: Hohosboco preserves an Indigenous waterway name from a 1662 meadow transaction. The boundary description points toward the Spring Creek landscape beside Jamaica Bay; the pin is approximate.
address_label: Present-day Spring Creek / Howard Beach, NY — approximate waterway location
map_geometry_source: Approximate historical association inferred from Riker 1852 p.53 and the 1910 Rockaway Park opinion; point on modern OSM waterway 998966842. Historical channel and meadow bounds not reconstructed.
why_this_matters: A creek name can preserve evidence of Indigenous people and land relationships even where urban construction has transformed the shore. Reading the boundaries alongside the named participants brings more of that history into view.
introduction_title: An Indigenous Name Beneath a Changed Waterfront
introduction_content: Hohosboco was a river named in the description of Plunder’s Neck, a salt-meadow tract on Long Island’s south shore. James Riker’s account of an October 3, 1662 transaction names the Indigenous participants Womatupa, Wonoxe and Powatahuman. Their names and the waterway survive in a record written around settlers’ acquisition of meadowland.1
history_content:
Riker places Hohosboco on the east of Plunder’s Neck and describes a smaller brook on its west flowing into that river. He explains that colonial farmers sought salt hay to sustain their cattle. The transaction therefore connects the Indigenous landscape with the material needs of an expanding settler economy.1

Tooker repeated the Hohosboco boundary in 1911. His entry gives no translation, so no meaning is assigned to the name here.2
whereintheworld_title: Location and Why the Pin Is Approximate
whereintheworld_content:
The pin sits on a mapped reach of modern Spring Creek near the Brooklyn–Queens border. The connection is an inference from two descriptions: Riker places Hohosboco east of Plunder’s Neck in 1662; a 1910 court opinion identifies the river east of Pleuders Neck in colonial patent boundaries as Old Seller River, Mill Creek and Spring Creek.1, 3

This supports the Spring Creek–Jamaica Bay area, but it does not establish the exact channel or meadow boundary of 1662. The chosen coordinate follows today’s mapped creek, not an excavated site, settlement or surveyed historical parcel.4

NYC Parks documents a landscape altered by roads, fill and other disturbance. Those changes make a present-day shoreline an imperfect guide to the older waterway. The dot is for orientation, not an access point; use designated public routes and observe posted restrictions.5
